Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Economy Ghana’s productive capacity has not been matched to finance growth, withstand external shocks – Cnergy Global Source : Joy Business 17 November 2026 2:33pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Cnergy Global Holdings has stated that though Ghana’s economic output has expanded strongly, productive capacity has not been matched by the capacity to finance growth, withstand external shocks, or generate secure, productive jobs.
In its review of the 2027 National Budget, it said the true test of a turnaround is how the 2027 Budget, particularly the New $10-billion Economy, changes these underlying relationships.
It said that while Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is trumpeted as a sign of good governance, its impact on citizens’ well-being is rarely assessed.
“Over the last 10 years, Ghana’s UNDP Human Development Index (HDI) has improved at a relatively subdued rate compared to 2001-2010. Weaker correlation factors include oil/gas and services expansion that did not raise labour earnings, COVID-19 health and education losses, the 2022/3 purchasing power decline, population growth and income distribution”, it pointed out.
Ghana ranks 143 of 193 countries in the latest UNDP report with a score of 0.628. Life expectancy of 65.5 years trails only Senegal, Gambia and Mauritania in the subregion. The country also ranks 2nd in West Africa on educational indicators, with expected schooling of 11.4 years and mean schooling of 7.1 years, but 125/193 for quality of education.
Interestingly, Cynergy Global said Ghana’s HDI score of 0.628 falls sharply to 0.399 (a 36.5% reduction) once adjusted for inequality, second only to The Gambia in the subregion.
“Thus, past “trickle-down” policies can be considered largely ineffective, except for the Free SHS, which directly impacted educational attainment (the worst-performing component). Continued investment in education and healthcare is required”, it added.
It continued that the ten-year record shows that while Ghana expanded real output by 55% between 2016 and 2025, and 2024–2026 stabilisation is meaningful, macro vulnerabilities can accumulate behind strong GDP numbers; commodity prices can improve trade balances without higher domestic production; and productive finance and decent jobs can lag GDP.
“Essentially, how effectively did higher production translate into greater purchasing power, longer and healthier lives, and more learning, and who received those gains?” its asked.
It stated that the answers will reflect whether growth impacts all aspects of the economy rather than creating prosperity silos for a few. “Converting growth to development is required to close the inequality gap and foster social cohesion”.
It also noted that the 2027 Budget should be scored by whether it reallocates scarce fiscal and administrative capacity toward investments and institutions that let firms and workers produce more and earn more to withstand the next shock.
